passage: Monday. After lunch, Vasudha, nine, left the school tap dribbling while she chatted with Parul. "One tap won't empty the tank," she said. Across the yard, other taps dribbled too. Wednesday. By the last period the tank was dry. Class 4 couldn't wash their tiffins, and the toilets smelled. The peon said every tap had been left open a little. Vasudha went quiet. She had thought it was only hers. Friday. Vasudha and Parul made signs in fat crayon: "Close me! Every drop is ours." They taped one above each tap. At break Vasudha caught herself about to walk away, and turned the tap off with a firm twist.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Parul write on the signs?
qa.a: "Close me! Every drop is ours."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha go quiet on Wednesday?
qa.a: She realised her dribbling tap was one of many, and felt guilty for thinking only hers wouldn't matter.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha and Parul make on Friday, and why could it help?
qa.a: They taped signs above each tap, reminding everyone that every drop is shared, so each person turns the tap off.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Class 4?
qa.a: They couldn't wash their tiffins and had to put up with smelly toilets, paying for everyone's dribbling taps.

grounding: A girl leaves a school tap running, sure one tap cannot matter, until everyone doing the same empties the shared tank.

passage: Jeevan Dadu pointed his stick at the green pond. "Rashmi, when I was ten, you could see fish in that water. Every child in the village swam there after school. And every one of us threw our sugarcane peels and paper in it. I used to think, 'My peel is so small. What difference can it make?' Everybody thought the same. One summer the water turned green and smelly. The fish floated up, belly first. The panchayat closed the pond, and we had nowhere to swim. That summer was long and hot and sad. That's why I still pick up peels along the bank."

qa.q: What did the children throw into the pond?
qa.a: Sugarcane peels and paper.

qa.q: What did young Jeevan think about his own peel?
qa.a: He thought it was so small it couldn't make a difference.

qa.q: What choice does Jeevan make now because of that summer?
qa.a: He still picks up peels along the bank, having learned that everyone's small peels together ruined the pond.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see a single wrapper after hearing this story?
qa.a: Rashmi may see it as part of a pile made by everyone, not a harmless little thing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, he and every other child littered a village pond thinking one peel didn't matter, until it was spoiled.

passage: The colony had one good cricket bat, bought with everyone's pocket money, and dark clouds were rolling in. Jatin, eleven, got it first and wouldn't let go. "Just one more over. Then Ramesh." Ramesh waited. So did the others. When Jatin was finally out, Ramesh grabbed the bat and kept it just as long. Then the next kid did the same. Nobody passed it on. They yanked it back and forth, arguing, and it slipped onto the wet concrete in the first drops of rain. The handle cracked. They stood in the drizzle, staring at it. "I only kept it a bit," Jatin muttered. "So did we all," said Ramesh.

qa.q: How was the colony's cricket bat bought?
qa.a: With everyone's pocket money.

qa.q: What was Jatin thinking in muttering 'I only kept it a bit'?
qa.a: Jatin felt that one person's extra time was too small to be the cause, not seeing that everyone had thought the same.

qa.q: What could the children agree on to protect the next bat?
qa.a: A fixed number of overs each, with the bat passed on in turn, so no one needs to hog it.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's reply 'So did we all' show about how Ramesh sees what happened?
qa.a: Ramesh sees that each of them took a little extra, and together that spoiled the bat they all owned.

grounding: Children each hog a shared cricket bat a little, thinking one person's share doesn't matter, until the fighting over it breaks the bat.

passage: The Class 5 paint tubs were bought with everyone's craft fund. On Monday Yamini, ten, squeezed out a huge blob of blue for a tiny sky, and left the lid off. "There's loads," she told Vaibhav. "My little bit won't finish it." Vaibhav squeezed out red the same way. So did the table behind them. Nobody put lids back, because nobody thought one open tub mattered. By Thursday the blue had a hard, cracked crust. The yellow was dry as chalk. When Ms Pinto announced the Independence Day posters, there was almost no paint left. Yamini poked the crust with her brush and said nothing.

qa.q: What did the paint tubs look like by Thursday?
qa.a: The blue had a hard, cracked crust and the yellow was dry as chalk.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel about using the paint on Monday?
qa.a: She felt unconcerned, believing her little bit would not matter because there was loads of paint, so she did not bother with the lid.

qa.q: What could Yamini do differently with the next set of shared paints?
qa.a: She could squeeze out only what she needs and close the lid each time, and suggest the class does the same, since the paint belongs to everyone.

qa.q: How are the rest of the class affected when the posters are announced?
qa.a: Everyone, including children who were careful, now has almost no paint for the Independence Day posters, even though the craft fund was theirs too.

grounding: A ten-year-old wastes class paint thinking her share cannot matter, everyone does the same, and the shared paint is spoiled for all.

passage: "Nirmala! Why is there no water in the bathroom?" Mummy called. "The whole building's tank is empty." Nirmala, eleven, looked at her little brother Tenzin. Tenzin looked at the ceiling. "We were washing our cycles on the terrace," he said. "With the hose," Nirmala added. "Only for a bit." "How long is a bit?" "Maybe... an hour? The Mehtas' kids were also doing it. And the boys from the fourth floor were having a water fight." Mummy sat down. "So everyone thought their bit was small." "One hose can't empty a whole tank, Mummy." "Five hoses can." Tenzin whispered, "Mrs Rao can't cook now, can she?" Nirmala felt her face go hot. "We could carry her a bucket from the corner tap."

qa.q: What were Nirmala and Tenzin doing on the terrace?
qa.a: They were washing their cycles with the hose.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels guilty once Mummy points out the problem?
qa.a: Her face goes hot when Tenzin mentions Mrs Rao, and she quickly offers to carry a bucket to her.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene could change how the children use the terrace hose?
qa.a: The moment Mummy says five hoses can empty the tank shows them their bit was not small, so next time they could use a bucket and stop quickly.

qa.q: How are neighbours like Mrs Rao affected by what the children did?
qa.a: Mrs Rao cannot cook because the whole building's tank is empty, even though she had nothing to do with the hoses.

grounding: An eleven-year-old and other children each waste the building's shared water thinking one hose does not matter, and the tank runs dry for everyone.
